            SOUTHWESTERN PUBLIC SERVICE COMPANY’S EXCEPTIONS TO
                       CERTIFICATION OF STIPULATION

        Southwestern Public Service Company (“SPS”) respectfully submits these Exceptions to

the Certification of Stipulation issued by Hearing Examiners Patrick Schaefer and Keven Gedko

on October 23, 2026 (“Certification”). 1 SPS appreciates the Hearing Examiners’ thorough review

of the Comprehensive Stipulation filed June 22, 2026 (“Stipulation”), including the evidence

presented at hearing. SPS supports most of the Certification, which recommends that the

Commission approve the Stipulation’s principal financial terms. Certain provisions of the

Certification, however, change the negotiated agreement among the parties, rely on inapplicable

cases, or fail to fully account for the evidence presented. Accordingly, as to these provisions, SPS

takes exception. These provisions include the Hearing Examiners’ recommendation that the

Commission:

        (1)      reduce SPS’s recoverable rate-case and regulatory expenses from $4,342,331 to
                 $3,338,676 and extend the stipulated two-year amortization of those expenses to
                 three years;

        1
           1.2.2.20(B)(5)(b) NMAC (“Exceptions to the certification may be filed within ten (10) days after the date
the settlement stipulation is certified to the commission, unless the commission or presiding officer directs
otherwise.”); see Certification ¶ 27 & n.40.



                                                         1
         (2)        disallow SPS’s $265,322 in annual Community Solar Portal operation and
                   maintenance (“O&M”) expense, which SPS expects to incur to administer its New
                   Mexico Community Solar Program;
        (3)        reject the stipulated methodology for calculating the accredited capacity benefit of
                   the Cunningham Battery Energy Storage System (“BESS”) when adjusting New
                   Mexico’s share of shared-system generation costs;
        (4)        reject the stipulated single-coincident-peak (“1-CP”) method for calculating the
                   system load factor used in the average-and-excess-demand four-coincident-peak
                   (“AED 4-CP”) customer class allocator; and
        (5)        replace the stipulated “Energy-at-Source” methodology for allocating production
                   tax credits (“PTCs”) to SPS’s customer classes with the AED 4-CP methodology.
        Accordingly, SPS respectfully requests that the Commission adopt the Certification subject

to these Exceptions and approve the Stipulation as filed.

                       I.   INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY OF EXCEPTIONS

        At issue is whether the Stipulation, considered as a whole, is fair, just, and reasonable and

in the public interest. In making that determination, the Commission considers whether the

Stipulation (1) resulted from serious bargaining among capable, knowledgeable parties; (2)

benefits customers and the public interest as a whole; and (3) violates any important regulatory

principle or practice. 2 The Commission may scrutinize disputed provisions, but “its ultimate

approval finding concerns the lawfulness and reasonableness of the stipulation as a whole.” 3

        The Hearing Examiners recognize that, “[c]onsidered as a whole, the Stipulation reflects a

negotiated accommodation of competing interests” and “substantially reduces SPS’s requested rate

increase.” 4 They conclude that the stipulated cost-of-service components “are supported by the

record and that the negotiated $90 million base-rate increase represents a reasonable compromise




        2
           Certification ¶¶ 28–31 (citing, inter alia, Case No. 24-00270-UT, Final Order ¶¶ 34–45 (Oct. 30, 2025);
Case No. 20-00238-UT, Final Order Adopting Certification of Stipulation in Its Entirety and Granting SPS’s Motion
for Reconsideration ¶¶ 6–7 (Feb. 16, 2022)); 1.2.2.20(B)(4) NMAC.
        3
            Certification ¶ 33.
        4
            Id. ¶ 8.



                                                        2
 of the Signatories’ competing positions.”5 On these points, the Hearing Examiners are correct. The

stipulated $90 million revenue increase is $85.4 million below SPS’s originally filed deficiency of

$175,354,544. It includes a $136,150 reduction to rate case expenses, a $235,602 reduction to

Community Solar costs, and $1,962,937 in additional non-defined reductions. 6 These concessions

reflect a Stipulation in which all Signatories agreed to give something up to achieve a good-faith

compromise.

         Yet the Certification recommends changing several negotiated terms, including the five

specific alterations challenged here, based on reasoning that, in several respects, overlooks record

evidence, misapplies ratemaking principles, or fails to account for the Stipulation as a whole.

Together, those changes would rewrite a carefully negotiated settlement whose terms the

Signatories expressly agreed are “interdependent and not severable.” 7

         First, the Certification unreasonably reduces the recoverable rate case expenses in the

Stipulation by a percentage derived from comparing SPS’s requested and incurred expenses in two

past rate cases. This selective comparison fails to account for either the much broader scope of this

proceeding or, importantly, the evidence of SPS’s actual expenses. For instance, SPS incurred

$2.26 million in its last rate case. Under the settlement in that case, SPS was authorized to recover

only $2 million. This left more than $260,000 in expenses unrecovered. Further, even though the

Signatories reached a Stipulation and avoided litigation in this case, doing so required extensive




         5
            Certification ¶ 142; See also id. ¶¶ 81–83 (rejecting Staff’s argument that Case No. 25-00066-UT precludes
SPS from using forecasted jurisdictional allocators); id. ¶¶ 88–93 (rejecting Staff’s challenge to SPS’s Future Test
Year under § 62-6-14(D)); id. ¶ 142 (finding that Staff failed to establish Future Test Year or linkage-data violations
sufficient to reject the stipulated increase).
         6
          SPS Ex. 48 (Johnson Reb. Support of Stip.) at 4–7, Table AMJ-STIP-R1; See also Staff Post-Hearing Brief,
Ex. A, Panel B (reproducing the same stipulated adjustments).
         7
           Stipulation § 2.7(b) (June 22, 2026) (providing that the Stipulation’s provisions are “interdependent and
not severable” and that no provision becomes operative unless the Commission approves the Stipulation in its entirety).



                                                          3
 written discovery, testimony from dozens of witnesses, a four-day evidentiary hearing, and

voluminous post-hearing briefing. 8 This process generated substantial costs. SPS has provided

invoices and itemized the expenses incurred to date, which support the Stipulation’s projected rate

case expenses. Besides unreasonably capping rate case expenses based on historical comparisons,

the Certification extends the stipulated two-year recovery period for those expenses to three years.

The Certification bases this change on speculation that SPS might delay its next rate case, despite

testimony that SPS expects to file another case in 2027. Neither the cap on rate case expenses nor

the extended amortization period for those expenses adequately reflects the evidence supporting

the Stipulation’s terms.

        Second, the Certification disallows the entire $265,322 in annual Community Solar Portal

O&M expense based on the mistaken premise that SPS failed to support the expense with

testimony. SPS did. SPS witness Zoë Lees expressly testified that SPS supported the O&M

expense through its cost-of-service materials and workpapers, including the materials SPS

identified in its post-hearing briefing. Although Staff questioned the detail supporting the estimate,

it did not dispute SPS’s statutory obligation to administer the Community Solar Program.

Additionally, in Case No. 23-00071-UT, the Commission authorized SPS to defer costs incurred

to implement the Community Solar Program, subject to later review. The Commission’s

Community Solar Rule likewise permits utilities to recover the administrative costs of carrying out

the program. The Certification recommends allowing SPS to recover those deferred regulatory and

IT costs, yet disallows the annual expense of operating the Community Solar Portal. The




         8
           Certification ¶¶ 229–242, 245–248; SPS Ex. 47 (Lees Rebuttal Testimony in Support of Comprehensive
Stipulation) at 60; Tr. Vol. I at 98:3–99:9, 116:19–117:1 (Lees); Stipulation § 1.10.



                                                     4
 Certification overlooks record evidence and fails to explain why concerns about the level of

supporting detail warrant disallowing the entire Community Solar O&M expense. 9

         Third, the Certification overstates the Cunningham BESS’s capacity benefit for

jurisdictional allocation purposes. It proposes reducing New Mexico’s share of system peak

demand by Cunningham’s full accredited capacity, rather than adjusting for seasonal planning

reserve requirements. The Hearing Examiners reason that the Southwest Power Pool already

accounts for planning reserves when calculating resource adequacy requirements. But resource

adequacy requirements and peak demand used in jurisdictional allocation measure different things.

Southwest Power Pool requires SPS to maintain enough capacity to serve peak demand and meet

its planning reserve margin. The 12-coincident-peak (“12-CP”) allocator, by contrast, measures

each jurisdiction’s contribution to system peak demand when allocating shared generation costs.

Southwest Power Pool’s reserve requirements do not increase New Mexico’s measured peak

demand under the 12-CP. As SPS witness Alexander Trowbridge explains, the stipulated method

for determining the Cunningham BESS’s capacity benefit converts the battery’s accredited

capacity into an equivalent reduction in New Mexico’s peak-load responsibility. Conversely, using

the full accredited capacity, as the Certification recommends, would overstate that offset and

improperly reduce New Mexico’s share of shared generation costs. 10

         Fourth, as to customer class allocation, the Certification rejects the stipulated method for

calculating SPS’s system load factor – the ratio of average system load to peak system load –



         9
          Certification ¶¶ 136–142, Finding (8)(e), Finding (9)(a)(i); Stipulation § 1.7(c); SPS Ex. 47 (Lees Rebuttal
Testimony in Support of Comprehensive Stipulation) at 63–64; Allison M. Johnson, Direct Testimony, Attachment
AMJ-8; SPS workpaper “SPS K&M Community Solar Portal TY Adj”; SPS Post-Hearing Brief at 49–50 & n.156;
17.9.573.13(D) NMAC.
         10
            Stipulation §§ 1.3, 1.17; Certification ¶¶ 204–209, 215–228; SPS Ex. 49 (Trowbridge Rebuttal Testimony
in Support of Comprehensive Stipulation) at 11–13 (explaining why the stipulated PRM adjustment properly measures
Cunningham BESS’s capacity benefit for purposes of the 12-CP allocator).



                                                          5
 without adequately considering the robust protections the Signatories negotiated for residential

customers. The Stipulation uses the 1-CP method to calculate the system load factor but keeps the

underlying AED 4-CP methodology for customer class allocation. The Hearing Examiners

recommend rejecting this change because it would shift approximately $2.3 million in allocated

costs to residential customers. But the Stipulation also reduces SPS’s requested revenue

requirement by $85.4 million overall and provides $28.5 million in gradualism support for

residential customers, substantially offsetting that shift. Moreover, the Signatories agreed to hold

stakeholder workshops to examine future class-allocation methods as SPS’s generation mix

changes. Taken together, these provisions make the stipulated system load factor calculation

reasonable. The Certification’s approach might also be reasonable, but the existence of a

reasonable alternative does not make the Signatories’ preferred approach unreasonable. 11

         Finally, the Certification would modify the Stipulation’s allocation of PTCs across

customer classes. It would allocate the value of those tax credits using the methodology used to

allocate generation costs generally, rather than the energy required to serve each customer class.

This rewrites the Signatories’ agreed allocation method and overlooks the way in which utilities

generate PTCs. Federal law ties PTCs to the amount of qualifying electricity a facility produces

and sells. The Stipulation’s Energy-at-Source method for allocating PTCs reflects this. It allocates

PTCs according to the electricity SPS must generate to serve each customer class, adjusted for line

losses. It also preserves the energy-based method SPS already uses to allocate PTC benefits. The

Certification would supplant the Energy-at-Source method with AED 4-CP allocation on the

theory that PTC benefits should be allocated according to each class’s share of renewable



         11
            Stipulation §§ 1.1, 1.11; Certification ¶¶ 43, 150–163, 193; Tr. Vol. II at 471, 476, 479–480 (Trowbridge).
See also Certification ¶ 154 n.202 (acknowledging that the $2.3 million residential cost shift is offset by $28.5 million
in gradualism support).



                                                           6
 generation costs. While this is a reasonable cost-causation theory, it does not make the stipulated

energy-based approach unreasonable. Indeed, the Hearing Examiners acknowledge that arguments

support both methods. At bottom, the record supports the Signatories’ negotiated approach and

should be approved, without modification, on that basis. 12

         In summary, the Certification’s changes to the Stipulation’s recoverable rate case expenses

and Community Solar Portal O&M alone would reduce SPS’s annual revenue requirement by

approximately $1.3 million, before gross-up. 13 The remaining proposed changes would alter the

agreed allocation of costs and benefits among jurisdictions and customer classes. While some of

the Certification’s proposals present viable alternatives, they do not justify departing from the

parties’ negotiated compromise. The Commission should reject the recommended modifications

and approve the Stipulation as filed.

                                      II.    STANDARD OF REVIEW

         As mentioned above, in reviewing a contested Stipulation, the Commission must determine

whether the Stipulation, considered as a whole, is fair, just, and reasonable and in the public

interest. In making that determination, the Commission considers whether the Stipulation (1)

resulted from serious bargaining among capable, knowledgeable parties; (2) benefits customers

and the public interest as a whole; and (3) violates any important regulatory principle or practice. 14


         12
             26 U.S.C. §§ 45(a), 45Y(a)(1); Stipulation § 1.11; Certification ¶¶ 164–184, Finding (9)(e)(iii); Richard
M. Luth, Direct Testimony at 29:9–16, Case No. 22-00286-UT (explaining the energy-based allocation of FPPCAC
costs and Hale and Sagamore PTC benefits among customer classes); Case No. 17-00044-UT, Final Order Adopting
Certification of Stipulation with Modification, Ex. A § XII(B) (Mar. 21, 2018) (approving crediting Hale and
Sagamore PTC benefits through the FPPCAC).
         13
            Stipulation § 1.10; Certification ¶¶ 140, 244, 248, 250. The stipulated $4,342,331 amortized over two
years equals approximately $2,171,166 annually; the recommended $3,338,676 amortized over three years equals
$1,112,892 annually. The difference, combined with the $265,322 Community Solar Portal O&M disallowance, is
approximately $1,323,596 annually before gross-up.
         14
           Certification ¶¶ 28–31 (citing, inter alia, Case No. 24-00270-UT, Final Order ¶¶ 34–45 (Oct. 30, 2025);
Case No. 20-00238-UT, Final Order Adopting Certification of Stipulation in Its Entirety and Granting SPS’s Motion
for Reconsideration ¶¶ 6–7 (Feb. 16, 2022)); 1.2.2.20(B)(4) NMAC.



                                                          7
 The Commission may scrutinize disputed provisions, but “its ultimate approval finding concerns

the lawfulness and reasonableness of the stipulation as a whole.” 15

        Consistent with this approach, which the Certification describes as “both granular and

holistic,” the Commission must evaluate disputed provisions in the context of the parties’ broader

compromise. A provision may impose greater costs on one customer class but remain reasonable

when other provisions mitigate those costs. The existence of another reasonable approach does

not, standing alone, justify revising the parties’ negotiated terms. Although the Commission may

modify a contested stipulation, it must support any modification with record evidence and consider

its effect on the agreement as a whole. 16

        Here, the Certification recognizes the correct standard but does not consistently apply it.

As explained below, it overlooks evidence supporting several stipulated provisions, favors

alternative approaches without establishing that the negotiated terms are unreasonable, and gives

insufficient weight to the concessions supporting the Stipulation as a whole. Accordingly, the

Commission should modify the Certification consistent with these Exceptions and adopt the

Stipulation as written.

                                            III.     EXCEPTIONS
        A.         Exception No. 1: The Commission should approve the stipulated $4,342,331 in
                   rate-case and other regulatory expenses to be amortized over two years
                   (Certification ¶¶ 229–244, 249–250; Finding (9)(d)(i) and (ii)).

        SPS’s Application requested $3,175,594 in rate case expenses for this proceeding and

$1,166,736 in other regulatory expenses, for a total of $4,342,330. 17 The Stipulation reduced the




        15
             Certification ¶ 33.
        16
            Certification ¶¶ 27–34; 1.2.2.20(B)(4)–(5) NMAC; Case No. 24-00270-UT, Final Order ¶¶ 34–35, 44–57
(Oct. 30, 2025).
        17
             SPS Ex. 2 (Lees Direct) at 64, 66 & Attachment ZEL-7; Certification ¶ 230.



                                                         8
 annual amount in SPS’s cost-of-service model by $136,150. 18 The Certification allows the

$1,166,736 in other regulatory expenses less $30,000, but reduces this case’s expenses to

$2,201,940 by first removing $200,000 of “Other Company Expenses” and then applying a 74%

factor derived from Case Nos. 22-00286-UT and 20-00238-UT. 19 The Certification also extends

the stipulated two-year amortization period to three years. The first substitutes a historical discount

drawn from materially different proceedings for SPS’s evidence of actual and projected costs; the

second extends recovery based on speculation that SPS will delay its next rate case.

              1.          The Certification’s 26% reduction in rate case expenses rests on flawed
                          historical comparisons rather than SPS’s evidence of actual costs.

        In reducing SPS’s stipulated rate case expense recovery by 26%, the Certification relies on

the expenses SPS incurred in two past rate cases, Case Nos. 22-00286-UT and 20-00238-UT. 20

Those cases were materially less expensive. Case No. 22-00286-UT involved a contested

stipulation, but CCAE was the only party to file a statement of opposition, and its objections

focused on a limited set of issues. CCAE opposed the stipulation’s provisions regarding SPS’s

operation of the Tolk Generating Station, NOx allowance recovery, and extension of the Nichols

gas plant’s service life. 21 CCAE presented the testimony of one witness to support its position.22

        In contrast, here Staff opposed most of the Stipulation – including the revenue requirement

– and presented the testimony of five witnesses over a multi-day hearing, followed by two rounds

(136,150)”); See also Staff Ex. 12 (Brossy Opposition to Stip.) at 7 (cost-of-service model originally included
$2,307,315 annually).
        19

 of post-hearing briefs and these Exceptions. 23 The contested issues are complex. They include the

ratemaking treatment of federal production and investment tax credits, jurisdictional and class cost

allocation issues, and recovery of significant new investment to serve customers. The substantially

broader scope of this proceeding belies the central premise of the Certification’s reduction to SPS’s

rate case expenses: that SPS should incur the same proportion of its estimated expenses as in the

earlier cases.

        The Certification’s reliance on SPS’s incurred rate case expenses in Case No. 20-00238-

UT is also problematic because the stipulation in that case was uncontested, which resulted in a

streamlined approval process. In addition, the Certification calculated the ratio of estimated and

incurred costs by dividing SPS’s incurred expenses of $2,004,417 by a request of $2,701,744. But

the Certification itself recognizes that the $2,701,744 request in Case No. 20-00238-UT “included

$377,560 in unrecovered rate case expenses from Docket No. 19-00170-UT.” 24 Those carry-over

dollars did not form part of SPS’s estimate of the cost of litigating Case No. 20-00238-UT. Rather,

they were previously approved, unrecovered balances from an earlier case. The Certification does

not explain how including those carry-over expenses produces a reliable measure of SPS’s

historical forecasting accuracy. Because the Certification treats SPS’s two prior cases as “no better

comparisons,” 25 the reliability of each comparison matters. A ratio of initial estimates to final costs

in two earlier cases, with different issues and different procedural paths, does not establish that

SPS’s estimate for this case is unreasonable.

        Nor were SPS’s expenses in this case purely prospective, as SPS provided real-time cost

data. Ms. Lees testified that SPS provided invoices supporting a portion of the rate case expenses

 in this case, and that SPS’s supplemental discovery response itemized the expenses incurred to

date. 26 To date, SPS has incurred $3,834,781 in rate case expenses, which already exceeds the

limit included in the Stipulation. Ms. Lees also explained that much of a rate case’s cost is incurred

“just before, during, and after the Public Hearing,” so that a substantial share of actual costs

necessarily is not known when the case proceeds to hearing. 27 Applying an across-the-board 26%

reduction to an amount that includes incurred costs, and that does not capture the post-hearing

work the Certification anticipated, does not produce a more accurate forecast.

              2.          The Certification improperly relies on a prior settlement amount rather
                          than actual rate case expenses.

        The Certification separately reasons that “$2,000,000 in 2022, adjusted for inflation to

2026, is approximately $2,289,242,” and that inflation therefore does not explain a request of

$3.175 million. 28 But the $2,000,000 figure was the negotiated recovery amount included in the

stipulation in Case No. 22-00286-UT rather than SPS’s original request or its actual expenses.29

The Certification’s own figures show SPS actually incurred $2,260,181 in that proceeding. 30 Thus,

SPS incurred more than $260,000 in expenses that the settlement did not authorize it to recover.

Adjusting that negotiated cap for inflation does not make it a reliable measure of the reasonable

expenses of this more complex proceeding.

        Finally, SPS does not ask the Commission to shift any burden. SPS supported its estimate

with sworn testimony and an itemized attachment, as the New Mexico Supreme Court permits.31

 Other than the $230,000 in specific items, Staff identified no component of the estimate as

is a reasonable, record-supported estimate and should be approved.

              3.       The Certification exacerbates the impact of its reduction by disallowing
                       specific expenses before applying the 26% historical adjustment.

        The premise of the 74% reduction in rate case expenses in the Certification is that SPS’s

cost estimates in past rate cases, taken as a whole, exceeded what SPS ultimately spent. Before

applying this reduction, however, the Certification disallows $230,000 in specific expenses,

including for “Other Company Expenses”. This itemized reduction duplicates the percentage

reduction and results in an overreduction of rate case expenses. That is, after disallowing $230,000

in specific expenses, the Certification then applies a 26% reduction to the remaining forecast

without identifying a separate, case-specific reason for that reduction. 32 The Commission should

not adopt this recommendation. Nevertheless, if the Commission removes the $200,000 and

$30,000 items Staff challenged, then no further percentage-based reduction is warranted.

              4.       The Certification extends the stipulated amortization period based on
                       speculation about SPS’s next rate case.

        Section 1.10 provides for recovery of rate-case and other regulatory expenses over two

years and allows SPS to seek authority to continue recovery of any unamortized balance if new

rates take effect before the two-year period ends. 33 The Certification extends the period to three

in unsupported company expenses labeled ‘Other,’” and then separately reducing the remaining FTY expense by 26%.
Staff Ex. 12 (Brossy Opposition to Stip.) at 7–8.

 years on the ground that a two-year period “would lead to over-recovery if the rates established in

this docket stay in effect for more than 2 years.” 34

       The only record evidence on timing supports a two-year amortization period. The

Certification acknowledges that if rates take effect in December 2026 and SPS files its next rate

case one year later, “the rates set in this proceeding would stay in effect for approximately two

years.” 35 That is precisely what the record shows. Ms. Lees testified that SPS “will be coming in

for a Rate Case likely next year,” given the infrastructure investments SPS must continue to make

to serve customers and accommodate growth. 36 Ms. Johnson testified that amortization periods are

set to align with the period in which SPS anticipates filing its next case, and that two years is

reasonable where SPS expects to file within that time. 37 No party offered contrary evidence. The

Certification’s three-year period instead rests on the hypothetical that SPS might “choose[] to delay

that rate case filing by a year.” 38 A modification to a negotiated term should rest on record

evidence, not speculation.

       The three-year period also shifts risk asymmetrically to SPS. The Certification describes

its approach as one that “tends to error in being too long,” with any shortfall addressed by allowing

SPS to seek continued recovery in its next case. 39 But the Certification is explicit that this “does

not automatically approve that future recovery.” 40 Meanwhile, SPS earns no return on the

       E.       Exception No. 5: The Commission should approve the stipulated Energy-at-

       The Stipulation reasonably allocates production tax credits (“PTCs”) among customer

classes based on the electricity SPS must generate to serve them. The Certification instead

recommends allocating PTCs based on the costs of the generating facilities that produce them.

Both methods are reasonable, but utilities earn PTCs from electricity generation, not capital

investment. The agreed Energy-at-Source method better reflects that distinction, follows SPS’s

existing practice, and represents a reasonable compromise among the Signatories. The

Commission should approve it.




                                                  23
              1.      The stipulated Energy-at-Source method reasonably allocates PTCs based
                     on the electricity that generates them.

        New Mexico law requires rates to be just and reasonable, and the Commission has directed

that allocation methods reflect actual system usage, benefits, and cost causation. 63 The same

principle supports allocating PTC benefits according to the activity that generates them. For PTCs,

federal law supplies that connection. The Internal Revenue Code calculates PTCs based on the

kilowatt-hours (“kWh”) of qualifying electricity a facility produces and sells. 64 Capital investment

makes generation possible, but the credits depend on electricity produced, not dollars invested or

retail prices charged. Energy use therefore provides a more direct basis for allocating PTC benefits

than a class’s share of generating costs.

        Section 1.11 applies that principle. SPS begins with each class’s metered electricity use,

adjusts for line losses at the voltage level serving that class, and allocates PTCs according to each

class’s share of the resulting generation requirement. Lower-voltage customers receive a

correspondingly greater PTC benefit per metered kWh because serving them requires more

generation. 65

        The Stipulation also preserves the Commission-approved treatment of Hale and Sagamore

PTCs. In Case No. 17-00044-UT, the Commission approved a stipulation requiring SPS to credit

Hale and Sagamore PTC benefits to New Mexico customers through its fuel and purchased power

cost adjustment clause (“FPPCAC”). 66 SPS allocates those benefits among customer classes on an
